1.1: 1.1 All wisdom, etc. RAB. in Ecclesiasticus, vol. 3. He begins with the eternal wisdom of God, which is Christ, who is always with the Father before the ages, according to the text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God (John 1). It is from the Lord God. For Christ, the fountain of life and the true light, is born of the Father, and all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (ibid.). Whoever lacks this wisdom walks in darkness and does not know where he is going. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, and the prudence of the flesh is death (Wisdom 11).
1.2: 1.2 The sand of the sea and the drops of rain. RAB., as above. He compares bodily things with spiritual things, so that what is wholly impossible may be estimated from things most difficult. For if no one can number these things, which were established in fixed number, measure, and weight, how much less will anyone be able to search out the wisdom of God, which is without beginning and without end, unutterable and beyond all estimation?
1.4: 1.4 Wisdom was created before all things. Created according to the humanity, in the counsel of God the Father; that is, it was predestined to be incarnate for the salvation of the human race. It should be noted, however, that on account of the unity of the person Christ is sometimes called begotten, sometimes created.
1.5: 1.5 The fountain of wisdom. The origin of all wisdom proceeds from the Word of God, who, God from God, remains always with the Father in the heavens; but having entered the world through the dispensation of his humanity, he gave commandments of salvation, whence: You have the words of eternal life (John 6).
1.6: 1.6 The root of wisdom. He shows that no one can penetrate the depth of God, or the greatness of his goodness and mercy. Hence, for the liberation and enlightenment of the human race, he deigned to become man, whence: Who shall declare his generation? (Isaiah 53).
1.9: 1.9 He himself created her. That is, he arranged the coming of the Only-begotten, through the Word co-eternal with himself and the Holy Spirit: how he would come through the Virgin's childbearing for the salvation of the world, and restore creatures, and call man back to the knowledge and love of himself, giving him the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that by his gift he might be set free forever.
1.11: 1.11 The fear of the Lord is glory, etc. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he delights exceedingly in his commandments. Glory and riches are in his house (Psalm 3), etc. The fear of the Lord. There are two kinds of fear. Of the one it is said, There is no fear in charity (1 John 4), etc. Those who have this fear cease to sin on account of dread of hell, and amend their life: it introduces charity, but is itself cast out. For he who fears in this way does not yet love or desire good things, but guards against evil; yet he amends himself and begins to desire good things. Of the other it is written, The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever (Psalm 18). For each one fears lest he lose the good things, and the presence of God, which he desires to enjoy forever, of which it is said:
1.12: 1.12 The fear of the Lord will delight the heart. This gives inward sweetness, and in the future eternal life.
1.14: 1.14 Love, RAB. The charity of God is true wisdom, etc., down to: the reward will be in the future itself; whence: You will fill me with joy with your countenance; delights are at your right hand for ever (Psalm 15), etc.
1.17: 1.17 The fear of the Lord. Without the fear of God and the keeping of his commandments there is no religion; whence: If anyone thinks himself to be religious, not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, this man's religion is vain (James 1).
1.19: 1.19 To him who fears the Lord. That is, to him who, by the fear of God, keeps the rule of righteousness in faith, teaching, and action.
1.23: 1.23 And he saw. RAB. All things are in his sight; he preserves for each one a worthy recompense.
1.25: 1.25 Branches. Through wisdom man has the divine knowledge of avoiding evil and the understanding of doing good, for each is wrought in the hearer in the end; whence: He who hears me shall not be confounded, and they that work by me shall not sin. They that explain me shall have life everlasting (Ecclesiasticus 24). The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding to all that do it (Psalm 110).
1.26: 1.26 In the treasures. In meditation on the law both are made clear: how evils are to be avoided, how spiritual wisdom is to be learned, and how good works are to be practiced, in which true religion consists. The understanding of wisdom. This forbids sins and carnal desires; whence: The pestilent man loves not one that reproves him, nor will he go to the wise (Proverbs 15).
1.27: 1.27 Fear, etc. Because through penance it cleanses from past sins, or restrains from sins about to be committed. For he who does not amend himself through the fear of God falls into the abyss of sin.
1.30: 1.30 A good sense. Whence in Proverbs: The lips of the wise keep them (Proverbs 14). And elsewhere: The prudent man does everything with counsel; but the fool has laid open his folly (ibid. 31). It is therefore the part of a wise man to hold his words and to carry out everything with moderation. They will declare his sense. With an even mind, rendering not evil for evil, but good for good.
1.33: 1.33 My son, desiring wisdom. Wisdom herself shows how you may come to wisdom, because without the preservation of righteousness no one reaches the summit of wisdom; whence James: Who is a wise man, he says, and endued with knowledge among you? Let him show, by a good conversation, his work in the meekness of wisdom (James 3).
1.34: 1.34 For wisdom and instruction. RAB. As has often been said, The fear of the Lord is the guard of wisdom and instruction (Proverbs 13), to which right faith and moderation of conduct are suited, because without faith it is impossible to please God, and the life of the good is always tranquil; whence in Matthew: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest to your souls (Matthew 11). For he who truly fears God cannot be without faith and good works, which fill a man with virtues and make him acceptable to God. Whence: To a man that is good in his sight, God has given wisdom, and knowledge, and joy. But to the sinner he has given vexation and superfluous care (Ecclesiastes 2).
1.36: 1.36 With a double heart. A man double in mind is inconstant in all his ways, who wishes, that is, to rejoice with the world and reign with Christ.
1.37: 1.37 A hypocrite. Bearing one thing in his heart and showing another in his deed. Whence: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep (Matthew 7).
1.38: 1.38 Take heed of them, etc. It is plain that whoever follows heretics acquires damnation for his soul, because at the judgment the secrets of hearts will be revealed, and to each one will be rendered according to his works; for God will destroy all that speak a lie (Psalm 61). He who abominates the bloody and deceitful man; whence: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. And elsewhere: The lord of that servant will come and will divide him, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 24).
2.1: 2.1 Son, coming, etc. He has shown what is to be avoided; now he shows what is to be done, saying: Son, coming to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear. For he who wishes to abstain from the allurements of the world and to live piously in Christ suffers persecution. For while he prepares to gird himself for the divine service, he stirs up the devil's war against himself, and while he subdues some vices he struggles against others, and he is led by divine dispensation so that he may overcome and be overcome, lest he be exalted. But since humility and patience are necessary to him, there follows: Humble your heart, and endure, etc.
2.4: 2.4 Keep patience. As if to say: In your patience you shall possess your souls (Luke 21), because patience is the root and guardian of all the virtues. It must be known, however, that patience is exercised in three ways. For we are scourged by God, but we must take care not to murmur; from our neighbor we endure persecutions, losses, and insults, and we must take care not to repay evil for evil; we are tempted by the adversary, but we must take care not to be bent toward delight in sin or consent to it, or to seek present things in exchange for these, but to await future things.
2.6: 2.6 Believe God and he will recover you. RAB. The afflicted man must believe, and direct the steps of his works into the sight of God, and hope in him; whence: Commit your way to the Lord, and trust in him, and he will do it (Psalm 36). Hence Jeremiah says: Blessed is the man that trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence (Jeremiah 17), etc.
2.7: 2.7 You that fear the Lord, etc. The Lord takes pleasure in them that fear him, and in them that hope in his mercy (Psalm 146). For he who truly fears patiently awaits his mercy: But they that forsake God shall be confounded and shall be written in the earth (Jeremiah 17).
2.8: 2.8 You that fear the Lord, believe him. He exhorts those who fear the Lord to believe him, so that they may come to a sure reward; whence: For the just man lives by faith (Romans 1); whence: Be of good heart, son, your sins are forgiven you (Matthew 9). And elsewhere: Your faith has made you whole (ibid., 10).
2.9: 2.9 You that fear the Lord, hope in him. He commends three things to those who fear God: to believe, to hope, to love; for God is truly worshipped by faith, hope, and charity, and one comes to contemplation, which is eternal happiness.
2.11: 2.11 Look upon, etc. RAB. Here too he says three things, etc., down to: a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit (Psalm 50), etc. And: The Lord is nigh unto all that call upon him in truth (Psalm 144).
2.14: 2.14 Woe to them that are of a double heart, etc. He has warned that no one should approach God with a double heart; now he says, Woe to the double heart and to wicked lips. For he who thinks and speaks perverse things and persists in perverse works, unless he repents, will perish forever. The one who enters the land by two ways is he who does evil and hopes for good; or he who follows the works of the flesh and supposes that he is perfecting the sanctification of the spirit in fear; or he who displays in deed what belongs to God and seeks in thought what belongs to the world. Such men are indeed inconstant in all their ways, because they are easily frightened in adversity and ensnared in prosperity.
2.15: 2.15 To the dissolute of heart, etc. RAB. He still teaches how to guard against error, etc., down to: but to them that do not submit to the truth, but believe iniquity, wrath and indignation, etc.
2.17: 2.17 To look upon, etc. Although God looks upon all things at every time, he is nevertheless said to look upon them when he is recognized as approving or disapproving something.
2.18: 2.18 They that fear the Lord will not be incredulous, etc. Alternating, he treats of the love and affection of God, because the holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever (Psalm 18), and everyone that loves is born of God and knows God (1 John 4). But he who truly fears God, and loves, and believes the Scriptures, keeps the precepts of God by acting on them, and by constant meditation seeks what is pleasing to him; he will therefore be filled with the wisdom and charity of God. For the end of the commandment is charity, and he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.
2.20: 2.20 They that fear the Lord will prepare, etc. Happy the soul that daily cleanses its heart to receive God as its inhabitant; whoever possesses him lacks no good, because he has within himself the author of all good things. And because for this the keeping of the commandments and patience in good work are necessary, by which one comes to the knowledge of the truth, there follows: They that fear the Lord keep his commandments, etc. The just man is the first accuser of himself. For as a reward remains for humility, so punishment remains for pride; whence John: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1). He who is truly wise is a true cultivator of righteousness, because wisdom dictates the rule of righteousness.
3.2: 3.2 The judgment of the father. Of God, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. Because all things are from him. He loves the things he has made, so that they may remain in him by whom they were made; whoever hears his judgment and does his commandments will be saved. His commandment is that reverence be shown also to the earthly father and mother; whence: Honor your father (Deuteronomy 5), etc.; whence there follows: He that honors his father. The honor that God has established for him ought not to be dishonored by his children, because God by his judgment will inquire how his precept is kept.
3.4: 3.4 He that loves. That is, he who keeps the commandments and abstains from sins, and yet does not cease to pray for transgressors, because he knows that the merciful judge hears prayers at every time.
3.6: 3.6 In his children. RAB. In offspring or in disciples, etc., down to: to honor parents is the first commandment with a promise.
3.9: 3.9 In work and word, that is, not in the womb; from which it is shown that the spiritual father too is especially worthy of honor; whence Paul: Through the Gospel I have begotten you (1 Corinthians 4). And elsewhere: Let the priests who rule well be esteemed worthy of double honor, especially they who labor in word and doctrine (1 Timothy 5).
3.11: 3.11 The blessing of the father, etc. RAB. The patriarchs blessed their sons, etc., down to: the mockers most savagely tore to pieces.
3.15: 3.15 Almsgiving. That is, that which blots out sin. For the sacrifice offered for sin is called sin. But he who has mercy on his parents or on other poor persons will receive the reward of righteousness, absolved from sins. Blessed are the merciful, for (Matthew 5), etc. And elsewhere: He that has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord (Proverbs 19). Hence Daniel to Nebuchadnezzar: Let my counsel be acceptable to you, O king: redeem your sins with alms, and your iniquities with works of mercy to the poor (Daniel 4), if perhaps God may forgive your offenses. Hence the Lord says: Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you (Luke 11).
3.19: 3.19 My son, in meekness. Meekness and humility bring forth grace; pride and fury bring forth ruin; whence: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11), etc. And elsewhere: He that exalts himself shall be humbled (Luke 14), etc.
3.21: 3.21 The greater you are, etc. RAB. He taught meekness above, etc., down to: it is enough for a man to think devoutly on those things, and to fulfill in deed what God has commanded.
3.24: 3.24 In superfluous matters, etc. RAB. That is, do not search superfluously, etc., down to: those who dispute fall into errors and depart from the truth.
3.27: 3.27 A hard heart. Because according to your hardness you treasure up to yourself wrath against the day of judgment (Romans 2).
3.28: 3.28 A heart entering. This is the one who takes no care and makes no effort to avoid, and who loves the things that lead to destruction, such as heresies and profane novelties; whence there follows: A heart entering two ways shall not have success, etc.
4.1: 4.1 Son, the alms of the poor man, etc. RAB. How much almsgiving avails, etc., down to: who rebukes from the heart by words or deeds.
4.3: 4.3 The heart of the needy, etc. Almsgiving is not to be deferred when the means of giving are at hand; whence: Say not to your friend: Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give, when you can give at once (Proverbs 3). And elsewhere: He that despises his neighbor sins; he that has pity on the poor shall be blessed (ibid. 14). But alms must be given not out of necessity: For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9). And elsewhere: The poor widow cast in more than all into the treasury, because God weighs not the quantity of the gift but the devotion of the heart.
4.5: 4.5 Turn not away from the needy, etc. The poor man is not to be exasperated by anger, but soothed with gentle speech, for the wrath of man works not the justice of God (James 1). And: He that stops his ear at the cry of the poor shall cry himself and shall not be heard (Proverbs 21). For he who can give ought to give: for a secret gift extinguishes anger, and a present in the bosom the greatest indignation. But he who cannot give: a good word is better to him than the best gift. But he who has the substance of this world, and sees his brother in need and shuts up his bowels from him, how does the charity of God abide in him? (1 John 3). For faith, if it has not works, is dead. Let us not therefore love in tongue and word, but in deed and in truth.
4.7: 4.7 To the assembly of the poor. In these words meekness and humility are commended, because meekness despises no one, and humility subjects itself to all. It befits a Christian to be affable and gentle to equals and inferiors, and humble to elders; whence: Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up (Psalm 130).
4.9: 4.9 Deliver, etc. RAB. As he said that largess to the poor is almsgiving, so he shows that the deliverance of one unjustly oppressed is mercy; whence: Deliver them that are led to death.
4.10: 4.10 In judging. RABANUS. No kind of alms, etc., down to so also be to widows a comfort of a husband.
4.13: 4.13 And they that shall watch, etc. Blessed is the man that hears me, and watches daily at my gates, and waits at the posts of my doors, Proverbs 8. By the doors he understands the Scriptures and their teachers.
4.15: 4.15 They that serve, etc. He who loves him that begot, will love him that is born of God, and whom the Father loves, the Son loves, whence: He that loves me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him. But because the proof of love is the showing of the work, it follows: He that hearkens to her shall judge nations. Whence: When the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Matthew 19.
4.19: 4.19 Fear and dread, etc. Wisdom dwelling in a man directs his works, in various temptations prepares by exercising and proving for the joys of the life to come, which is confirmed by this sentence: Fear and dread and trial, etc. Because tribulation works patience, and patience trial, and trial hope, which confounds not, because the charity of God is poured forth in the saints by the Holy Spirit.
4.23: 4.23 My son, observe the time, etc. Above he commended the gift of wisdom, now he shows its effect. For whoever keeps the precepts of wisdom is cautious in the change of times, nor forsakes the way of justice in the time of persecution and distress. Therefore wisdom exhorts her sons to observe the time, because there is a time for every thing under heaven: and a time of war, and a time of peace.
4.28: 4.28 Hide not your wisdom, etc. RABANUS. Wisdom is not to be hidden from those who wish to hear. For he that hides up corn shall be cursed among the people, but a blessing upon the head of them that sell; whence: Trade till I come, Luke 19.
4.30: 4.30 Gainsay not. Elders are to be obeyed, if they agree with truth and justice, and not otherwise, but for right faith and true religion, in which is the salvation of the soul, one must strive; whence: If your eye scandalize you, pluck it out and cast it from you, Matthew 5. And, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, Luke 9., etc.
4.34: 4.34 Be not hasty in your tongue. RABANUS. Death and life, etc., down to it is written: The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power, 1 Corinthians 4.
4.35: 4.35 Be not as a lion. In the Church there are heretics like lions, who by the volubility of the tongue seduce the hearts of the innocent, and by insolence of manners disturb the meekness of the simple.
5.11: 5.11 Winnow not yourself, etc. RABANUS. He reproves lightness, etc., down to the double-mindedness of their doctrine, in which they bring forth now true things, now false, shows them to be sinners.
5.13: 5.13 Be meek. It is good to hear meekly, and receive the word of truth, and bring it forth modestly and prudently; whence: Let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger, James 1. And a little after: Receive with meekness the ingrafted word, which is able to save your souls, ibid. In Proverbs also it is said: Have you seen a man hasty to speak? there is more hope of a fool than of him, Proverbs 29.
6.1: 6.1 Be not made, etc. RABANUS. He shows the force of true charity, etc., down to his virtue shall be dashed.
6.4: 6.4 Wicked. The fruit of good work follows good will, and nothing of prosperity a malicious mind. For if charity is lacking, you spend your effort in vain on virtue; whence: He that offends in one point is guilty of all, James 2. And, From him that has not, even that which he has shall be taken away, Luke 19.
6.6: 6.6 Be many at peace, etc. Peace is to be had with all, so far as our frailty permits, but not counsel with many, because it is written: Many are called merciful, but a faithful man who shall find? Proverbs 20.
6.7: 6.7 If you gain a friend, etc. RABANUS. Expressing false friends by diverse kinds, at length he comes to the true friend: because many profess themselves friends in prosperity, and appear enemies in adversity. Whence: If he humble himself against you, etc.
6.13: 6.13 Take heed. RABANUS. That is, have discretion, etc., down to: Now I beseech you, brethren, to mark them who make dissensions and offenses, Romans 16.
6.14: 6.14 A faithful friend. A friend a sharer in love, to whom so apply your mind that of two there be made one, to whom commit yourself as to yourself, of whom fear nothing: and ask nothing dishonorable. For friendship is not venal, but full of honor; whence: You are my friends if you do the things that I command you, John 15., etc. The Lord gave us the form of friendship which we should follow, that we do the will of a friend, open to him secrets, and he to us; whence: But I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you, ibid.
6.16: 6.16 A faithful friend. According to God, namely. He treats with a friend of what is necessary to the remedy of eternal life and immortality: whence Cicero says friendship can be only among the good, and friendship ought to be free, and inclined to all felicity.
6.17: 6.17 He that fears the Lord. RABANUS. The full and perfect grace of friendship, etc., down to that you believe you will be departing this world daily.
6.27: 6.27 With all your mind. RABANUS. With the heart, not the body, one must approach wisdom, etc., down to the perception of truth; whence: This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, John 17., etc.
6.33: 6.33 My son, if you will. Wisdom admonishes that we meditate assiduously on the divine law. First she exhorts that we learn; next, that we apply the soul to it, then, that we incline; finally, that we apply diligence to hearing. For so wisdom promises to make the wise. For it is necessary that he who desires the knowledge of true wisdom, which is Christ, first humbly subject himself to Catholic masters, and all the affections of his soul to their discipline. Then, turning the intention of the heart from every perverse desire, let him diligently apply it to hearing the word of God, and beware to bestow meditation of the law not for the reward of earthly things, or human praise, but for love of the good itself, that he may receive the fruit of true wisdom.
6.35: 6.35 In the multitude. As: Be not wise to yourself. Trust not your own wit, the pride of heretics chiefly tripped them up.
6.37: 6.37 Think upon the commandments. RABANUS. Deservedly it is given to him, etc., down to and assiduously meditates the law and carries it out in work.
7.1: 7.1 Sow them not in the furrows of injustice, and you shall not reap them sevenfold. RABANUS. Perfect vengeance, etc., down to He takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, Luke 11.
7.4: 7.4 Nor of the king the seat of honor. He cannot exercise the work of just rule who has neglected the sentence of true piety; whence: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you not so, but he that is greater among you, let him be as the younger, Luke 22.
7.5: 7.5 Because he is the knower. No presumption is more pernicious than to be proud of one's own justice or knowledge; whence: There is no man upon earth who does good and sins not, Ecclesiastes 7. And elsewhere: Have you seen a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him, Proverbs 26.
7.6: 7.6 Seek not to be made a judge, unless you have strength. Everyone ought to weigh his own virtues, and according to the quantity of his strength take the care of others: lest while he delights in the place of glory, he become to subjects the author of ruin; and he who is burdened by the weight of his own, wish to become the judge of others' faults.
7.7: 7.7 Offend not against the multitude. He who is strong in reason and prevails by the power of free will should not sin by the insolence of subjects, but constantly resist the wickedness of others: nor think he sins with impunity if he acquiesces in the will of the many; whence: Not only they that do them, but they also that consent to them that do them, Romans 1., etc.
7.13: 7.13 Be not willing to make any manner of lie. Every lie is evil; and to bring scandal on neighbors is pernicious. Much more then to plot fraud against a friend, to lay a charge: for a lying witness shall perish; whence in Proverbs: As he is guilty who shoots arrows unto death, so is he that hurts his friend by fraud, Proverbs 20.
7.15: 7.15 Be not full of words. As: Do not teach your own sense, hear the wisdom of the elders. For it is safer to hear than to speak; whence: Let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger, James 1. Hate not laborious works. To sinning man knowledge was given, that by the labor of his hands he might seek his living; whence: In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, Genesis 3., etc.
7.19: 7.19 For the vengeance on the flesh, etc. Because the flesh of sinners, which flows away in luxury, will be tormented by the fire of hell and worms, where the worm dies not, and the fire is not quenched: in the worm the rottenness of Gehenna, in the fire the burning is signified. Or the worm is the late repentance of crimes, which in torments ceases not to bite the conscience of sinners, so that fire is punishment raging from without, but the worm a grief accusing from within.
7.20: 7.20 Prevaricate not against a friend for money. RABANUS. Many have perished for avarice, etc., down to: He that hates gifts shall live, Proverbs 1.
7.21: 7.21 For the grace of modesty. Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for them that love him. By this woman wisdom can be understood, which elsewhere is called the precious pearl, which the spiritual merchant finding sells all things and buys it. Whence: Live joyfully with the wife whom you love; as, follow wisdom, and the knowledge of the Scriptures, and join it to you as a spouse.
7.22: 7.22 Hurt not the servant. How servants are to be nourished is plainly shown, with the affection of sons by the right of nature; and to be disciplined for the instability of mind; whence in what follows, Food and a rod and burden for an ass; bread and discipline and work for a servant.
7.23: 7.23 Nor forsake him that is in want. Oppressed by the violence of servitude. For whether servants or free, we are all one in Christ, 1 Corinthians 12.
7.26: 7.26 Daughters, etc. As good servants are to be held with the affection of sons, so maidservants as daughters, he teaches, but with discipline: whence, Give your son the breast, and he will make you afraid: play with him, and he will make you sorrowful. Laugh not with him, lest you grieve, and in the end your teeth be set on edge, Ecclesiasticus 30.
7.28: 7.28 A woman. He commends conjugal chastity, removing every detestable union. Mystically, however, he admonishes that holding firmly the Catholic faith in true religion, which we first obtained after receiving baptism, we reject the perfidy of heretics.
7.32: 7.32 Love, etc. RABANUS. The fear of God and love, etc., down to because charity covers a multitude of sins.
7.35: 7.35 The gift of the arms. Above for what is offered to the ministers of God he promised the purging of sins: now for alms pardon and the grace of blessing, because as water quenches fire, so alms quenches sins.
7.37: 7.37 And to the dead. Burial of the dead belongs to alms, much more therefore consolation of the living: whence Paul teaches to rejoice with them that rejoice, to weep with them that weep. The proof of love is the showing of the work: whence, He that has the substance of this world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels from him, how does the charity of God abide in him? 1 John 3.
8.1: 8.1 Strive not with a mighty man. RABANUS. A proud one. Whence, Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be made like him, Proverbs 26.: because among the proud there are always quarrels, but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel.
8.2: 8.2 A rich man. He who pants with the heats of avarice. For thence arise envies, contentions, and the like, For the root of all evils is covetousness, 1 Timothy 6.
8.13: 8.13 Kindle not the coals. THE SAME. Whence the Apostle: If a man be overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness, Galatians 6.
8.15: 8.15 Lend not. RABANUS. Whence: Drink water of your own cistern, and the streams of your own well, have them alone.
8.17: 8.17 Judge not against a judge. As: be subject to prelates and judges who judge according to God.
9.1: 9.1 Be not jealous over the wife, etc. RABANUS. He teaches chastity, etc., down to does not consent to heretical perversity.
9.3: 9.3 A woman of many wills. The synagogue of heretics, which flits through diverse errors.
9.4: 9.4 Use not much the company of a woman that is a dancer. The crowd of heretics, which leaps through diverse errors, to draw to herself like a harlot whom she sees a lover of her eloquence; whence: She entangled him with many words, and drew him with the flattery of her lips, Proverbs 7., etc.
9.5: 9.5 Gaze not upon a virgin. Turn away your eyes, that they behold not vanity: let it not please you to see what it is not lawful to covet. Mystically, however, we ought not to love the beauty of heretical eloquence, nor attend to feigned virtues.
9.7: 9.7 In the streets of the city, etc. The same under another figure. For the streets of the city are the conventicles of heretics: which separate themselves from the city, of which it is said: Glorious things are said of you, O city of God, Psalm 86.
9.14: 9.14 Forsake not an old friend. Greater is the confidence from a thing known than unknown. The doctrine also of the holy Fathers we ought not to decline and hear new teachers.
9.15: 9.15 New wine, etc. A new teacher ought to study to receive sound doctrine and working firmly: and afterward to profit himself and others.
9.25: 9.25 A talkative man. A heretic, who is always contentious, and therefore hateful to God and men.
10.1: 10.1 A wise judge, etc. RABANUS. The government is made upon his shoulder. Whence: Woe to the land whose king is a child, Isaiah 9., the devil, namely, who always loves novelties, and whose princes eat in the morning, that is, before the day of death, saying: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die, Isaiah 22.
10.5: 10.5 Upon the face of the scribe. THE SAME. My tongue is the pen of a scribe that writes swiftly, because in his place he sends to preach.
10.8: 10.8 A kingdom from a nation. RABANUS. This almost all, etc., down to: The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof, Matthew 21.
10.9: 10.9 To the covetous. After the change of kingdom he treats of avarice, for which the force of rule is chiefly neglected: For the root of all evils is covetousness, 1 Timothy 6. Pride, however, accompanies avarice, whence, Charge the rich not to be high-minded, ibid.
10.12: 10.12 And the king is today. Power and riches cannot prolong life. A term is set which cannot be passed. The pleasantness of the flesh will be turned into rottenness and stenches, and at length into worms. Mystically, however, the man who lives in sins and repents not will die with eternal death: and will not escape the devil the old serpent and his beasts, that is, the demons.
10.14: 10.14 The beginning of pride. For there is no greater apostasy than that the creature depart from the Creator, which is rightly ascribed to pride. For it is pride if the creature wishes to be equal to the Creator. This was to both the devil and man the beginning of perdition: whence, For the beginning of all sin is pride. Although elsewhere it is said: The root of all evils is covetousness, 1 Timothy 6. There is no covetousness without pride, for no one is proud but covetous and conversely. From pride are born heresies, schisms, detractions, envy, wordiness, boasting, contentions and the like, which proceed from covetousness. The gluttonous, intemperate, drunkards, fornicators and the like are made by covetousness, which cannot be without pride. Let us beware therefore of covetousness and pride, not two evils, but one from which all draw their beginning.
10.19: 10.19 Lands. RABANUS. When Jerusalem by the Romans, etc., down to their posterity was blotted out, and the glory of the martyrs exalted; whence: The Lord keeps all them that love him, but all the wicked he will destroy, Psalm 144.
10.22: 10.22 Is not created. THE SAME. Vices were not created, etc., down to arises anger, which the constancy of virtue overcomes.
10.23: 10.23 The seed of men shall be honored. The holy teachers are in honor with the good, especially those who fear the Lord: whence, Let the priests that rule well be esteemed worthy of double honor, 1 Timothy 5., etc.
10.25: 10.25 The glory of the rich, etc. Truly the glory is to fear God. He who fears him keeps justice in all things: whence, Have not the faith of Jesus in respect of persons, James 2.
10.27: 10.27 The judge is great. Though earthly power be great, it cannot surpass him that fears the Lord: for to them that fear God nothing is wanting, The rich have wanted and have suffered hunger, Psalm 33., etc.
10.28: 10.28 A wise servant. This literally often happens, that one ignoble in birth is preferred to the noble by the knowledge and faith of nobility: whence, A wise servant shall rule over foolish sons, Proverbs 17. Mystically, however, the ecclesiastical servant, who devoutly keeps the Christian religion, is preferred to the Synagogue; whence, The elder shall serve the younger. And, Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated, Genesis 25.
10.30: 10.30 Better is. As if to say: It is better that you study always to labor in good work, whence the reward of justice is rendered to you, than that you consume your days in vanity, and want that bread which came down from heaven. He who in fear of God and observance of religion will establish his glory: whence, He that glories, let him glory in the Lord, 2 Corinthians 10.
11.1: 11.1 The wisdom of the humbled shall lift up his head. It follows: Praise not a man, etc. As if: Judge not the quality of the mind by the appearance of the body: whence, Look not on his countenance, nor on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him, nor do I judge according to the look of man, 1 Kings 16. For man sees those things that appear. But the Lord beholds the heart. In worldly honors one must not be proud, because the world passes away and the concupiscence thereof.
11.5: 11.5 Many tyrants. RABANUS. It is done by divine dispensation, etc., down to inherited the blessing of the patriarchs.
11.8: 11.8 Before you hear. He who answers before he hears, that is who desires to be a teacher before he learns; or to judge the causes of others before he discerns, shows himself a fool.
11.10: 11.10 My son, meddle not with many things, etc. As if he said: Be not curious about superfluous things, and consent not to the perversity of sinners. For not only they that do evil, but they who consent to the doers are worthy of death. My son, meddle not with many things, etc. Many are the acts of heretics, who keep not the unity of faith, and the path of truth, and spend one labor in composing books. Copious in rhetoric and dialectic art: nor are they free from the beloved, because their meditation is in guile. Whence Ecclesiasticus: My son, make not many books, of which there is no end. All the books, however, of divine Scripture, because they agree, are one book: whence, In the head of the book it is written of me, Psalm 36., etc. My son, meddle not with many, earthly gains, or any businesses, because to one intent on many the sense is less for single things. He who has undertaken the care of rule is found unequal to single things while he is divided among many: nor considers his own losses while he handles another's.
11.11: 11.11 There is a man that labors. He designates Christian works, in which the poor in spirit abound in all good things, and those who labor in acquiring riches are in want: whence, The rich have wanted and have suffered hunger, etc.
11.18: 11.18 There is one that grows rich, etc. RABANUS. He lays up treasure, and knows not, etc., down to but they leave to others who discern truth and falsehood.
11.30: 11.30 Before death, etc. THE SAME. It is foolish to praise, etc., down to who come in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
11.32: 11.32 For as they belch, etc. RABANUS. The likeness of the more cunning animals, etc., down to into the cage of error and snare of deception they cast down.
12.3: 12.3 For it is not, etc. It is a most grave sin to be unwilling to repent, nor to redeem sins by alms, but to add sins to sins: whence, For three crimes of Damascus, and for four I will not convert her, Amos 1. The doubtful and deceitful doctrine which they bring forth in the exposition of the divine Scripture.
12.5: 12.5 Give to the good, etc. Something like it is read in Tobias: Lay out your bread and wine upon the burial of a just man, and do not eat and drink thereof with sinners, Tobias 4. That is for the reason that they are sinners, do not communicate; as those who feed actors while the poor of Christ are hungry. But he who gives to a needy sinner, not because he is a sinner but because he is a man, feeds not the sinner but the just: because he loves not the fault, but the nature. If he understands the sinner and impious heretic while they are in error, one must not communicate with them: whence, Give not that which is holy to dogs, Matthew 7.
12.8: 12.8 A friend shall not be known in prosperity. More easily friend and enemy are proved in adversity, because there are many friends of the table, who abide not in the day of need. He was a true friend therefore who said: Who is weak, and I am not weak? 2 Corinthians 11.
12.10: 12.10 Never trust your enemy. Historically he treats of false friends, of whom we ought to beware. Mystically, however, he marks heretics, who are not truly friends, whose doctrine is full of the rust of error and wickedness: whose speech creeps like a cancer, though they feign themselves faithful and Catholic. Let us not therefore consent to them, nor give them power, which the right hand signifies: lest they cast us down from our place, that is, the state of right faith. For they strive maliciously to overthrow our chair, that is doctrine. Who shall heal. The heretic who bears the office of teacher, and says he is a physician of souls: For if the salt lose its savor, it is good for nothing any more but to be cast out, Matthew 5.
12.15: 12.15 In his lips. By these sentences he marks those who speak in the heart and lie in wait to kill the innocent: who when they have deceived someone, shake the head, clap the hand, and rejoice when they have done ill.
13.1: 13.1 He that touches pitch shall be defiled. RABANUS. By a similitude he shows, etc., down to lest the evils they frequently behold they wish to imitate.
13.2: 13.2 He lifts a burden upon him. THE SAME. These instruct us morally to follow humble things, flee proud: For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, James 4. Mystically, however, he teaches, etc., down to because they will show themselves worthy of eternal confusion, when they shall be tormented forever.
13.11: 13.11 Be not, etc. He does not abhor the virtue of humility: but teaches to hold firm authority against the assailants of truth, whom one must strongly resist.
13.12: 13.12 An advocate. One must deal modestly with the powerful of this world, who frequently deride the simplicity of the innocent: to whom nevertheless we ought to give due honor, but not against God, or against his commandments. Whence, Honor all men, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king, 1 Peter 2.
13.16: 13.16 Take heed to yourself, and attend. As: nothing is safe with lovers of the world, who follow changeable things and are changed with them. Whence: A fool is changed as the moon, Ecclesiasticus 27. Heretics and false Christians can be understood in these, who are not to be believed, because they are inconstant in all their ways.
13.18: 13.18 Every living thing. RABANUS. The others refuted, etc., down to because the Lord is nigh unto all that call upon him in truth.
13.19: 13.19 Every beast. He looks to the above, that you decline the society of the rich and powerful, and be joined to him who is your partner in zeal and religion. For this is firm friendship, which likeness of virtues allies. If it shall communicate. The rapacity of the wolf agrees not with the innocence of the lamb, nor the rage of the avaricious with the modesty of the simple. For there is no communion of cleanness with uncleanness: For as a dog returns to his vomit, so is a fool that repeats his folly, Proverbs 6. There is no parity therefore of the proud rich man with the humility of the poor of Christ.
13.25: 13.25 The rich man moved. What he rebukes about the rich and the poor, he follows up: because there are many who extol the deeds and words of the rich: few who understand the teaching and virtue of the humble. The arrogant find preachers, but the humble scorners. Whence: Riches make many friends, but from the poor man, even those whom he had are separated, Proverbs 19.
13.31: 13.31 The heart of a man changes. In the judgment of the countenance, the change of mind is detected: whence, A glad heart makes a cheerful countenance, in sorrow of mind the spirit is cast down.
13.32: 13.32 The sign of a good heart. Because many are feigned and pretended: therefore it is hard to find one in whom the heart and face, that is thought and operation and doctrine, agree in good: when however you find this, give glory to God, because this is his gift.
